materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.046J S15 Lecture 1: Overview, Interval Scheduling

notes.summary: 6.046J is 6.006's graduate sibling: fewer topics, deeper proofs, taught by Moshkovitz with full video. Lecture 1 frames the course (intractability will be the destination) and solves interval scheduling with the earliest-finish-time greedy — a canonical proof of optimality by the 'greedy stays ahead' exchange argument.
notes.focus: Rewrite the interval scheduling proof yourself: induction showing the greedy's i-th pick finishes no later than any alternative's. If you can reproduce it cold, the whole proof style is yours.

lessons.title: Divide and Conquer: Convex Hull, Median Finding

notes.summary: Divide-and-conquer beyond mergesort: the convex hull in O(n log n) by sorting-then-merging hulls, and deterministic selection (median) in O(n) via groups-of-five recursion. The master theorem is introduced as the standard tool for analyzing the resulting recurrences.
notes.focus: Analyze the median-of-medians recurrence on paper. The magic is that the 70-30 split makes the recursion tree's work geometric — understand why 3 fails and 5 works.

notes.summary: Amortized analysis done rigorously: the aggregate, accounting (bank), and potential methods, demonstrated on two-pointer tables and binary counters. This formalizes the intuition from 6.006's dynamic arrays and is the exact machinery splay trees will need later — potential functions become a real tool, not a trick.
notes.focus: redo the binary counter with the potential method, defining Phi explicitly. Writing a VALID potential function is a skill — practice it now, splay trees will demand it.

notes.summary: Randomness as an algorithmic resource. Freivalds' trick verifies matrix multiplication in O(n^2) with one-sided error; randomized quicksort gets expected O(n log n) with no assumptions about input order. The expectation arguments use your Stat 110 linearity training directly — probability courses and algorithms meet here.
notes.focus: redo the randomized quicksort expectation argument. Note exactly where linearity is used — it is the same move as Stat 110's indicator tricks.

lessons.title: Randomization: Skip Lists and Universal Hashing

notes.summary: Skip lists get O(log n) expected search with random towers instead of rotations — elegance over cleverness. Universal and perfect hashing (lecture 8, reading) go deeper than 6.006: perfect hashing achieves worst-case O(1) lookups for a static set, showing what randomness buys when you can afford two-level tables.
notes.focus: Compute the expected height of a skip list tower yourself (geometric distribution). Your Stat 110 geometric distribution knowledge is a prerequisite here — use it.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.046J S15 Lecture 9: Augmentation, Range Trees

notes.summary: Augmenting data structures: store extra per-node data (subtree sizes, min/max) and maintain it under updates. Order statistics (select the k-th smallest) in O(log n), and range trees answering orthogonal range queries. The design rule: augment with what your queries need, and prove the augmentation survives rotation.
notes.focus: Add order-statistics to your 61B AVL mental model: which rotations change which subtree sizes? Walk one insert and update the augmentation by hand.

notes.summary: DP at graduate level: longest palindromic subsequence, pretty printing with line breaks, and knapsack, each with careful subproblem design and reconstruction. The lecture emphasizes the analysis craft — counting subproblems and work per subproblem — and when memoization beats cleverness.
notes.focus: For knapsack, state the running time in two variables (n, W) and explain why pseudo-polynomial is not polynomial. That distinction returns in the NP lectures.

notes.summary: MST theory done with proofs: the cut property (some minimum-weight edge crossing every cut is safe) powers both Kruskal and Prim. The union-find structure from 61B gives Kruskal its near-linear cost. Dijkstra falls out of the same greedy framework — a unified theory of greedy correctness.
notes.focus: Prove the cut property in your own words. It is short, and it certifies BOTH MST algorithms — one theorem, two algorithms.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.046J S15 Lecture 13: Max Flow, Min Cut

notes.summary: Flow networks and the max-flow min-cut theorem — one of the most beautiful dualities in CS. Ford-Fulkerson's residual-graph iteration is proved via the augmenting-path argument. Matching problems (lecture 14) reduce to flow, connecting graphs to assignment problems.
notes.focus: Run Ford-Fulkerson on a small graph and draw the residual graph after each augmentation. The final cut you find IS the min cut — see both sides of the duality in one drawing.

notes.summary: Linear programming as a universal optimization language: maximize a linear objective over polyhedral constraints, solved (geometrically here) by simplex vertex-hopping. Standard form, duality, and translating problems — diet, flow, and max strategies — into LP is the skill. LP solvers power real industry optimization.
notes.focus: Translate max flow into an LP yourself. Once you see flow constraints are linear, every other reduction in the lecture becomes mechanical.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 6.046J S15 Lecture 16: P, NP, NP-Completeness

notes.summary: The cliff edge of the course: P, NP, polynomial reductions, and Cook-Levin — SAT is as hard as anything in NP. Then the classics: 3-SAT to vertex cover to set cover via reductions you reproduce by hand. Knowing a problem is NP-complete changes your job: stop seeking exact algorithms, start approximating (lecture 18, reading).
notes.focus: Memorize one reduction chain: 3-SAT to independent-set to vertex-cover. Reproducing a chain by hand is exactly what complexity exams test.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the algorithm design toolbox: greedy with proofs, divide-and-conquer with recurrences, randomized analysis, amortized analysis, and DP. 6.046J tests proofs, not implementations — work the exams writing full arguments, and grade yourself on proof structure, not final answers.
notes.focus: Write one full exchange argument under a 20-minute timer. The skill is fluency under pressure, and only repetition under time pressure builds it.

notes.summary: The close: approximation algorithms (vertex cover factor-2, set cover ln n) as the constructive response to NP-completeness, randomized algorithms as a third paradigm, and the course synthesis. Your one-page map from 6.006 grows a column: 'or prove it hard, then approximate.' The theory courses (6.045J) formalize the cliff you just met.
notes.focus: Write the vertex cover approximation proof (pick both endpoints of a maximal matching). Short, constructive, and satisfying — a good final artifact for the term.
